 The cost of opportunity: federal student loan policy and gender inequality
 How new loan restrictions could affect women, female-dominated professions and access to higher education 
 Categories: 
 Opinion 
 by Samantha Bretz , Opinion Reporter 
 November 6, 2026 
 Katie Wang University of Wisconsin Office of Student Financial Aid. February 11, 2024. 
 President Donald Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act into law July 4, 2025. As laid out in the bill, the U.S. Department of Education and the president are implementing a new policy for financial aid. The policy will be implemented in 2027 and will halt students in lower-paying fields from receiving college loans. It will also require undergraduate programs to disclose the financial information of their students to see the contrast in salaries between different education levels. 
 Graduate programs will be required to reveal whether their graduate students will earn more than someone who has a bachelor’s degree. If their obtained degrees show a lack of earnings compared to someone with only a high school diploma or bachelor’s, they will not qualify for the William D. Ford Federal Direct Loan program — the largest federal loan program — which acts as a lender for postsecondary education and funding, according to a DOE press release . 
 Congress reported that at the end of the third quarter of fiscal year 2024, $1.4 trillion in principal and interest on the Direct Loan was borrowed by 37.5 million individuals. Without access to this loan, there will now be constraints that minimize the ability for people to even have a financial opportunity to go to college. The main cohort of people that will be affected by this new standard will be people who pursue socially valuable careers: mission-driven roles and professions that improve a person’s well-being. In the public’s eye, these careers have been interpreted as spaces that mostly recruit women. 
 While the DOE has not specified what degrees will be under review and federal courts have blocked some federal actions, there have been inferences. A concern is that the degrees that will be most impacted are primarily female-dominated professions. Some of these professions include cosmetologists , dental assistants and   social workers , all of which are currently female-dominated . These statistics not only highlight the outright discrimination against women but also reinforce the interpretation of the public.

 The bill also targets a specific demographic of individuals who take out federal loans. According to the Education Data Initiative, around 60% of all student loans are taken out by women. So, is the fight against institutions and their prices or on keeping women out of the workforce? 
 The DOE declares the new policy is only trying to help bring down the prices of education. “The Trump Administration is implementing commonsense reforms that will drive down the cost of higher education,” Under Secretary of Education Nicholas Kent said in the DOE press release. If the government’s main concern is about how expensive universities are and the amount of debt the government is in because of student loans, shouldn’t they mandate lower prices of university? 
 Unfortunately, prices are only rising at universities. At the University of Wisconsin , the tuition is still going up. As of the academic year 2026-27, there has been a 2% increase in tuition for students in residence and a 4% increase for non-residential students. The UW System Board of Regents also approved a 2.4% increase in segregated fees at the school. Due to the price increase, only a select few can afford the prices for the 2027 academic year. 
 The people who rely on federal student loans in order to attend UW may not have that option anymore under the new policy. Is it up to the government to dictate and condition people’s rights to secondary education? According to the Higher Education Act of 1965 , it’s not — Title VII in the Higher Education Act authorizes grants for improved education and community service programs to foster innovation in postsecondary education.

 This act requires the government to foster innovation and higher education, yet now there are stipulations to education that should be attainable for everyone. The government should be focused on increasing access to education rather than deciding what degrees are worthy. 
 This new policy will cause irreparable damage to the demographic of people who cannot afford to get a secondary education and will affect the number of people in specific professions. People should not be punished for wanting socially valuable careers that require a bachelor’s degree to obtain a position. The government poses this policy as a way to lower prices at institutions, yet the prices keep surging and becoming more unattainable. 
 Is the purpose of this new policy to bring the cost of university down or to keep a demographic of people uneducated? If this policy is not to target women specifically, it is doing so inadvertently. The value of an education should not be determined by the size of a paycheck, nor should the opportunity to pursue one be limited by gender.
